title: The Tablighi Jamaat
hookLine: a worldwide movement of traveling preachers calling Muslims back to prayer

lines: WILL YOU COME TO THE PRAYER?
cards: Late afternoon, a doorbell rings. On the step are a few men you've never seen: one older, one barely out of college, one with a duffel bag over his shoulder. They're not selling anything.
They're not collecting money. They've come from another city, and they're sleeping on the floor of the local mosque this week. One smiles: we're just reminding our brothers about the prayer.
Maghrib is at the mosque tonight, with a short talk after. Will you come? Then they thank you and walk on to the next door.

teach.b: Tabligh means conveying, passing the message on. Jamaat means a group.
The movement began in Mewat, near Delhi, with a Deobandi scholar named Muhammad Ilyas Kandhlawi, who wanted ordinary Muslims, not only scholars, to carry the basics of faith and prayer to each other.

teach.h: OUT IN SMALL GROUPS, ON FOOT.
teach.b: Members volunteer to go out, in their own words, in the path of Allah, for a set stretch of time, in small groups.
They pay their own way, carry their own bedding, stay in mosques, cook and eat together, and take turns serving each other.

In the afternoons they walk the streets around the mosque, knocking on Muslim doors, inviting people back to the congregation. In the evenings they read together from collections of virtues and hadith.
The ground it stands on: the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation, "And there may spring from you a nation who invite to goodness, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency."

teach.h: CONVEY FROM ME, EVEN ONE VERSE.
teach.b: And al-Bukhari reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase: convey from me, even if it's a single verse. Tabligh is that conveying, done on foot.
The movement describes itself as staying out of politics and out of arguments between schools, and as speaking mainly to Muslims, not seeking converts. It has admirers and critics among Muslims.
Some praise how it brings people back to the prayer. Some scholars question parts of its reading books, or long absences from home, and members answer those questions in their own terms.

how: Members of the Tablighi Jamaat volunteer to travel at their own expense in small groups, stay in mosques, go door to door inviting Muslims to the congregational prayer, and hold readings from collections of virtues and hadith; the movement describes itself as non-political.

practice: Picture yourself with the duffel bag: a floor to sleep on, someone else's cooking, a street you don't know, a door you have to knock on.
Notice what comes up, nerves, curiosity, embarrassment, and then picture the other side of the door: someone who hasn't been to the mosque in years, hearing their name said kindly.
If you pray, remember the people who knock and the people who answer.

wordCard.voice: The Tablighi Jamaat. A movement of volunteers who travel in small groups, stay in mosques and knock on doors, calling Muslims back to the prayer. Today's word.
